claims.text: Applying a high-temperature treatment during synthesis will improve the structural stability of high-entropy nanoalloys relative to untreated high-entropy nanoalloys.
Applying a high-temperature treatment during synthesis will improve the chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys relative to untreated high-entropy nanoalloys.
High-temperature processing can be used during the synthesis of compositionally complex alloy nanoparticles.
The treatment will improve the lattice structure of high-entropy nanoalloys.
The treatment will improve metallic bonding in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Thermal stabilization of the lattice is the mechanism responsible for the predicted stability improvement.
Enhancement of metallic bonding is a mechanism responsible for the predicted stability improvement.
The predicted improvement should hold in high-temperature applications.
The exact treatment temperature and duration required for optimal stability are uncertain.
Failure of treated nanoalloys to show improved structural and chemical stability relative to untreated controls would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes unspecified high-temperature applications and says the exact treatment temperature is uncertain, yet gives a 60–120 °C boundary without clarifying whether it describes the synthesis treatment or application exposure; this range is also poorly aligned with the broad high-temperature framing.
